Chapter 4. Institutions as Machines of Discipline: Shaping Everyday Life.
Imagine walking through the halls of a school, past the wards of a hospital, along the rows of a factory, or inside the cells of a prison. You start to notice a pattern. Each place feels different on the surface—different rules, different routines, different ways of sorting and shaping the people inside. But underneath? The logic is surprisingly similar: discipline, order, and control.
You see, institutions are so much more than just buildings. Think of them as machines, designed to produce certain kinds of people. They take us in as individuals, and through a mix of routines, constant watchfulness, and correction, they turn us into students, patients, workers, or prisoners. The process is quiet, but it’s always at work.
Take the hospital, for example. A patient’s day is broken into rounds, meals, treatments, and set times for rest. Every symptom gets recorded. Every change is noticed. Over time, the patient learns to follow instructions, to undergo test after test, to become more of a case than a person. Hospitals don’t just heal—they shape how we behave, enforce routines, and, quietly, decide what counts as normal or healthy.
Schools do something similar. Kids are sorted by age, by ability, and by how they act. They move from one class to another, one subject to the next, always under the watchful eyes of teachers and staff. The lessons aren’t just about reading and math. Kids learn how to wait their turn, raise a hand, accept their grades and rankings. So, school shapes not just what we know, but who we become.
Factories run on these principles too. Workers are assigned specific tasks, tracked for efficiency, and either rewarded or corrected based on their performance. It’s about more than making products. The factory is a training ground, turning people into reliable, disciplined workers—habits that follow them long after they clock out.
And then there’s prison, maybe the clearest example. Every move is controlled. Every action is watched. The goal? To break old habits, build new ones, and turn lawbreakers into model citizens. But here’s the thing—the methods you find in prisons aren’t so different from those in schools, hospitals, or factories. They just look a little different from place to place.
Most of us go through these institutions without ever really questioning them. We accept the routines, the rules, and the constant monitoring as just the way things are. But the impact runs deep. These places don’t just react to disorder—they create order, set the standards for what’s normal, and punish anyone who doesn’t fit the mold.
The real power of institutions comes from making discipline feel totally natural—even inevitable. They promise progress, safety, and efficiency. But they also bring anxiety, competition, and that constant feeling of being watched and judged.
